title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbook Standards
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This document defines Redwood Inference’s standards for Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) artifacts: SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning procedures, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and runbook structure. The goal is consistent, measurable reliability expectations across services, clear ownership of error budgets, repeatable capacity planning, and high-quality post-incident learning.

Intended audience
- Service owners (Product/Engineering leads)
- On-call SREs and incident commanders
- Platform and infra teams responsible for monitoring and capacity
- Reliability program managers

Goals
- Ensure every externally visible service has an owner-defined Service Level Objective (SLO) and an associated error budget policy.
- Provide a standard, repeatable capacity planning cadence tied to business metrics.
- Require consistent incident review artifacts and timelines for learning.
- Standardize runbook format and operational tooling so on-call responders can act quickly and safely.

1) SLO and Error Budget Standards

Summary
An SLO expresses the target level of reliability for a service in measurable terms. Every customer-facing and platform service must publish at least one SLO that maps to user impact (latency, availability, correctness). Error budgets are derived from SLOs and are consumed when SLOs are violated; they drive operational behavior (rate limits, rollbacks, feature freezes, capacity purchases).

Required fields for an SLO page
- SLO id: unique short identifier (service-name.slo.primary)
- Owner: team and primary contact (email or pager)
- User-visible metric: e.g., request success rate, P95 latency for key API path, embedding delivery success rate
- Measurement window: 30d rolling recommended (can be 7d for high-frequency experimentation)
- Target: e.g., 99.9% availability, P95 < 120ms
- Error budget: computed as 1 - target over the measurement window and expressed as allowable minutes or percentage
- Measurement system: data source(s) and query used (Prometheus recording rule, production trace sampling config, or analytics event stream)
- SLO stakeholders and reviewers

SLO quality checklist
- Metric maps to user experience (not internal queues or debug-only counters).
- Measurement system has >99% fidelity for the metric; missing data handling documented.
- Alerting and dashboards exist for both SLI and error budget burn rate.
- Ownership is clearly named with a rotation or escalation path.

Example SLO table (text representation)
| service | user-visible metric | window | target | error budget |
| inference-api | successful responses for /v1/generate | 30d rolling | 99.95% | 0.05% (≤21.6 minutes/day) |
| embeddings | batch embedding job success rate | 30d rolling | 99.9% | 0.1% |

Error budget policy and actions
- Green (error budget >= 75% remaining): normal development and launches allowed.
- Yellow (error budget 50% - 75% used): limit high-risk launches, require a canary, increase monitoring cadence.
- Orange (error budget 75% - 90% used): freeze non-critical releases, schedule reliability-focused engineering work, and notify stakeholders.
- Red (error budget > 90% used or SLO violated): immediate rollback of suspect changes, paging meeting within 1 hour, and formal incident review triggered.

2) Capacity Planning Standards

Cadence and stakeholders
- Quarterly capacity planning sync owned by Platform + SRE with attendance from service owners, product PMs, and finance for large commitments.
- Monthly operational capacity review for immediate scaling events and near-term forecasts.

Inputs and outputs
- Inputs: historical RPS and token/sec metrics, growth forecasts from Product/GTN, performance profiles per model (tokens/second per GPU), quantization/packing improvements, expected launches (new models/features), and region-specific demand.
- Outputs: capacity commit plan (monthly/quarterly), scaling runbooks, cost vs. latency trade-off recommendations, and a risk register for capacity shortfall scenarios.

Procedure (quarterly)
1. Gather baseline utilization and peak-percentile stats (P50/P90/P99) by service and region.
2. Collect demand forecasts from product teams (expected user growth, marketing campaigns, model rollouts).
3. Map workloads to execution profiles (e.g., llama-2-70b fp16 at seq256 = ~X tokens/s on A100) and compute GPU-hour needs.
4. Identify capacity gaps and propose mitigations (reserved capacity, autoscale policy updates, model quantization, caching improvements).
5. Present plan to Finance for procurement/commits and to Exec for approval if cross-org trade-offs required.

Capacity planning table (text)
| service | current p95 tokens/s | forecast 3mo tokens/s | proposed GPU type | delta GPUs | action |
| inference-api | 12k | 18k | A100-80GB | +8 | add reserved capacity Q3 |
| reranker | 3.2k | 3.6k | T4 | +2 | enable burst autoscaling |

3) Reliability Initiatives and Roadmap

Program structure
- Reliability initiatives (RIs) are time-boxed projects that address systemic reliability gaps (e.g., prefix caching rollout, model fallbacks, multi-region failover). Each RI must include a hypothesis, measurable success criteria (SLO impact, cost reduction, MTTR improvement), owner, timeline, and a rollback plan.

Sample initiative template
- Title: Global prefix caching for inference-api
- Hypothesis: Caching common prefixes will reduce per-token compute by 15% and lower P95 latency by 30ms for conversational workloads.
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime / Platform
- Success metrics: reduce average token compute by 15% and decrease SLO burn rate by 40% over 90 days.
- Timeline: discovery 2w, implementation 4w, canary 2w, rollout 2w.

Prioritization criteria
- Expected SLO improvement or error budget recovery per engineering week invested.
- Customer impact severity and number of affected customers.
- Cost savings or capacity deferrals enabled.

4) Incident Review Standards and Timelines

Incident classification
- Sev 1 (P0): Customer-facing outage or SLO breach impacting >10% of customers or core regions; requires immediate page and dedicated incident commander.
- Sev 2 (P1): Degraded performance or partial outage; page on-call and start an incident thread.
- Sev 3 (P2): Minor degradation or single-customer impact; track and schedule remediation.

Incident review deliverables and deadlines
- Incident timeline and notes posted within 24 hours to the incident page.
- Initial incident review (blameless) draft within 72 hours covering timeline, root cause hypothesis, immediate mitigations, and action items.
- Full postmortem with corrective actions, owners, and target completion dates published within 7 calendar days for Sev1 and 14 calendar days for Sev2.
- Action items must be tracked in the reliability initiative backlog and linked to owners.

Postmortem quality checklist
- Clear timeline with timestamps and referenced monitoring graphs.
- Root cause analysis that reaches a corrective action (not just symptoms).
- Concrete, time-bound action items (owner + due date).
- Verification plan for each action item and criteria for closure.

5) Operational Tooling Standards

Core tooling (approved stack)
- Monitoring and metrics: Prometheus (node/service metrics), Cortex/Thanos for long-term retention, and Grafana for dashboards.
- Tracing: Jaeger/Tempo with sampling policies aligned to SLIs.
- Logging: Loki/Elastic for structured logs with retention rules.
- Alerting: Alertmanager with on-call routing rules and alert runbook links.
- Incident management and paging: PagerDuty integrated with status pages.
- Synthetic testing: k6/Locust for load tests and internal synthetics for endpoint availability checks.

Operational standards
- Every SLO must have at least one dashboard panel in Grafana and a daily/weekly synthetic test.
- Alerting thresholds are tied to SLOs or error budget burn rate; no pager alerts for informational events.
- All alerts must include a concise intent (what the alert is for), a runbook link, and suggested next steps.

Example alert template (short)
- Name: inference-api_high_error_rate_5m
- Intent: page when 5-minute error rate for /v1/generate exceeds 0.5%, indicating potential SLO breach.
- Runbook: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/inference-api-generations.json#high-error-rate
- Pager rule: page on-call inference-api primary, escalate to platform lead after 30 minutes.

6) Runbook Structure and Expectations

Canonical runbook sections (each runbook must include)
- Title and short description
- Owner and on-call rotation contact
- Triggers (alerts or symptoms that should consult this runbook)
- Immediate mitigations (step-by-step commands with expected outcomes)
- Safety checks and preconditions (e.g., do not restart services during migrations)
- Diagnostic commands and representative Grafana dashboards
- Rollback and recovery actions with validation steps
- Post-incident follow-up checklist linking to the incident review template

Runbook content examples (text snippets)
- Diagnostic command: kubectl -n inference-api get pods -l app=inference-api -o wide
- Check cache tiers: curl -sS http://cache-cluster.prod.internal/health | jq .status
- Temporary mitigation: enable model-fallback mode: POST /admin/config {"fallback": true} (only allowed if authorized)

Runbook publishing and maintenance
- Runbooks must be reviewed every 6 months by the owner and marked with the review date.
- Owners must update runbooks after any incident where the runbook was used, within 72 hours.

7) Ownership, Escalation, and Governance

Ownership model
- Primary: service team owns SLO definition, runbooks, and incident follow-ups.
- SRE/Platform: owns monitoring primitives, global dashboards, capacity planning facilitation, and on-call tooling.
- Reliability Council: cross-functional forum (monthly) to arbitrate SLO changes, approve large reliability initiatives, and resolve inter-service capacity disputes.

Escalation paths (example)
- On-call -> Service lead (if unresolved after 30 minutes) -> SRE manager -> Platform director -> CTO for executive-level incidents.

8) Compliance and Auditing

- SLOs, error budget burn histories, and postmortems will be archived for at least 3 years for auditability.
- Quarterly reliability metrics and an annual report will be shared with Exec and Finance.

Appendices
A. SLO calculation examples
- Availability SLO (percent success): SLO% = (1 - total_failed_requests / total_requests) * 100 over 30d rolling window.
- Error budget minutes: minutes_in_window * (1 - target) where minutes_in_window = 30 * 24 * 60 for a 30d window.

B. Quick checklist for service owners before launch
1. SLO created and published with measurement query.
2. Dashboards created and reviewed by SRE.
3. Runbooks written and linked to alert rules.
4. Capacity forecasted and reserved if required.
5. Canary plan and rollback procedure documented.

C. Useful links
- SRE runbook template: /confluence/eng-sre/templates/runbook-template.json
- Incident review template: /confluence/eng-sre/templates/incident-postmortem-template.json
- Capacity planning spreadsheet: /drive/shared/infra/capacity-planning-qbr-2026.xlsx

Document maintenance
- This standard is maintained by the SRE program team. Major revisions require Reliability Council approval. Minor updates can be published by the SRE program lead with reviewers notified.
